name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 3 June 1972

clue.text: Wings etc for return part of a journey

blocks.note: to come back is to return
a stage is one leg of a longer trip

explanation.surface: A traveller pays for the homeward leg of a trip, with 'wings' suggesting an aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suggests flight, but here they are the wings of a theatre stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The wings, dressing rooms and other areas hidden from the audience are all behind the scenes of a theatre.

clue.text: Make a move toward a financial statement

indicators.note: going toward a word but not reaching it means stopping one letter short of its end

blocks.note: a government's annual statement of spending and taxes

explanation.surface: Someone takes a step in the direction of drawing up the accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: BUDGE is everything of BUDGET up to the final T: the word is approached but not reached.
explanation.definitionFit: To budge is to shift position even slightly, typically used of something stubborn or immovable.

clue.text: A cleaner fib "my darling"

blocks.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British word for a woman paid to clean houses
a fib is a small untruth

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady tells a small lie, calling someone her darling.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from the Scottish Jacobite song 'Charlie is my darling', about Bonnie Prince Charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-known song title pairs the name with those words, so the quoted phrase points straight to the name.

clue.text: Seen through a glass clearly?

blocks.note: surface reading: a twist on St Paul's 'through a glass, darkly', about seeing something plainly
setter's reading: a sight or show, a thing seen, whose plural names the lenses that help you see clearly

explanation.surface: A reversal of the Biblical line about seeing through a glass darkly.
explanation.walkthrough: The singular is a sight or show; add an S and you have eyeglasses, the glass you see through.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is something seen, a striking sight, and spectacles are glasses that make vision clear.

clue.text: Scotland's pride of place at a round-table session?

definitions.text: Scotland's pride of place at a round-table session?

blocks.note: surface reading: a famous Scottish landmark, a hill overlooking Edinburgh
setter's reading: the chair King Arthur would occupy among his knights at the Round Table

explanation.surface: Scotland's place of honour at a conference held around a circular table.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh hill shares its name with the chair a legendary king would sit in at his Round Table.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct volcano above Edinburgh carries the legendary king's name, and the phrase also literally means the king's chair.

clue.text: R.A. at the breakfast table

blocks.note: surface reading: a Royal Academician, a distinguished painter, sitting down to breakfast
setter's reading: probably Ra, the Egyptian sun god, as a fried item served sunny side up

explanation.surface: A distinguished painter from the Royal Academy sits down to his morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The intended joke is uncertain; most likely Ra the sun god stands for the bright yellow yolk of something served sunny side up.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiled or fried one with its golden yolk is the classic item on a breakfast plate.

clue.text: If in an offer in two parts

indicators.note: placed in means one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: a bid is an offer of a price, here split around the other piece
taken as written

explanation.surface: A conditional bid made in two instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology a bifid structure is split or cleft into a pair of lobes or branches.

clue.text: Wild bears are inferior

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bears in the wild are lesser creatures than tame ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'are inferior' read as 'are more lowly', i.e. are of a lower sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Baser is the comparative of base, meaning lower in quality, rank or moral worth.

clue.text: Beast branded on the back

blocks.note: surface reading: an animal that has been marked with a hot iron on its back
setter's reading: a 'dog' of iron holding burning brands at the back of the hearth

explanation.surface: A farm animal marked with a hot iron on its back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Branded' suggests marking cattle, but brands are also burning logs, and the 'beast' is an iron support that holds them at the back of the fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: An andiron is a metal stand that supports logs in an open hearth, traditionally called a dog.

clue.text: Naval establishments tail off to some extent

blocks.note: to dock an animal is to cut its tail short
an extent measured out in units of three feet

explanation.surface: Naval bases are running down to a certain degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail off' looks like 'decline' but is the verb for cutting a tail; 'to some extent' becomes a measured distance.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipbuilding and repair yards run by a navy are among its main shore facilities.

clue.text: My love is no bargain obviously

blocks.note: first meaning: a term of endearment for a beloved
second meaning: the most expensive item, clearly not a cheap buy

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that a lover proves costly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: the costliest thing on offer is plainly not a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of dear means both most beloved and most expensive, giving a pet name and a pricey purchase.

clue.text: As much of that North Sea conversion sleight as we can stomach?

definitions.note: an adjective meaning relating to the stomach, read loosely from the phrase

indicators.note: taking only as much as can be swallowed means not quite all of the word, so the end is cut

blocks.note: Britain was then converting homes to natural fuel piped from North Sea fields
sleight of hand is a conjuring trick

explanation.surface: A grumble about how much of the North Sea gas conversion trickery the public can tolerate.
explanation.walkthrough: In the early 1970s British households had their cookers converted to North Sea gas. TRICK loses its K, as if only partly swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric means belonging to the stomach, as in gastric juices or a gastric ulcer.

clue.text: Brilliant success of Tooting Bee late-night show

indicators.note: to show is to put on display, so part of the run of words is exposed while the rest stays hidden

blocks.note: surface padding: part of the place name Tooting Bec, a district of south London
the printed 'Bee' is a misprint for Bec; its closing letters are kept
the opening letters of this word are kept
surface padding completing the phrase late-night show

explanation.surface: A late-night show in Tooting is a dazzling hit.
explanation.walkthrough: Tooting Bec is a district of south London; the archive text misreads its last letter as e. Read correctly, the answer is hidden across bEC LATe.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat, from French, is conspicuous brilliance of achievement or a dazzling effect that wins acclaim.

clue.text: Not like Mr Wiseman

blocks.note: surface reading: unlike some sage gentleman called Wiseman
setter's reading: Mr Worldly Wiseman, the smooth tempter in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, so 'not like' him means lacking his worldliness

explanation.surface: Someone is quite unlike a gentleman named Mr Wiseman.
explanation.walkthrough: The full name of Bunyan's character is Mr Worldly Wiseman; the clue drops his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unworldly means naive, spiritual or innocent of material and social cunning.

clue.text: They may be spotted breaking into trunks

definitions.text: They may be spotted breaking into trunks

blocks.clueFragment: They may be spotted breaking into trunks
blocks.note: surface reading: thieves who might be seen forcing open luggage

blocks.clueFragment: They may be spotted breaking into trunks
blocks.note: setter's reading: birds with spotted plumage that drill holes in tree trunks

explanation.surface: Burglars might be noticed forcing open travel chests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' suggests being seen, but the great and lesser spotted are species of these birds; the trunks are of trees.
explanation.definitionFit: These birds hammer holes in bark with their beaks to find insects and make nests.

clue.text: The Pict was drawn to this river

blocks.clueFragment: The Pict was drawn to this river
blocks.note: surface reading: an ancient Scottish tribesman was attracted to a river

blocks.clueFragment: The Pict was drawn to this
blocks.note: setter's reading: the word Pict, attached to the front of this one, makes a word for a drawing

explanation.surface: An ancient Pict found himself drawn to a particular river.
explanation.walkthrough: PICT + URE = PICTURE, and a picture is literally drawn. The Ure is a river in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ure is a Yorkshire river flowing through Wensleydale, a favourite crossword river.

clue.text: Torchbearer for would-be stargazers

blocks.note: surface reading: someone carrying a light for amateur astronomers
setter's reading: a cinema attendant whose torch guides filmgoers, who come to gaze at film stars

explanation.surface: Someone holding a lamp for people hoping to observe the night sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The stars are film stars, and the torch is the flashlight a cinema attendant used to show people to their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: She was a woman employed in a cinema or theatre to guide patrons to their seats in the dark.

clue.text: Sweet or a twin to give us a shakedown

definitions.note: a phrase describing the sugar's use rather than a noun

blocks.note: Castor and Pollux are the twins of Greek myth, the Gemini
sugar is the basic sweetener

explanation.surface: Someone sweet, or else one of a pair of twins, will give us a thorough search.
explanation.walkthrough: A castor is a pot with a perforated lid for shaking sugar over food, hence 'shakedown'.
explanation.definitionFit: This fine-grained British baking sugar is made to be sprinkled from a shaker over desserts and fruit.

clue.text: Earl of Pembroke, not Shaftsbury

blocks.note: surface reading: one noble title set against another
setter's reading: Shaftesbury suggests arrow shafts, so the contrast is the weapon that fires them, and a mighty one

explanation.surface: Telling apart two English earldoms, Pembroke and Shaftesbury.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard de Clare, second Earl of Pembroke, who led the Norman invasion of Ireland in 1170, was nicknamed this. Shaftesbury is another earldom whose name begins with shafts.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname belonged to the twelfth-century Earl of Pembroke, Richard de Clare, conqueror in Ireland.

clue.text: Stay-at-home? Home's stay

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who stays indoors keeping house
second meaning: the support or prop of a household, who keeps it running

explanation.walkthrough: The same words swap places and change meaning: 'stay' is first a verb of remaining, then a noun meaning a support.
explanation.definitionFit: This person manages a household's domestic affairs, both remaining indoors and holding the place together.

clue.text: Like Antony stripped by Eros after all was lost

definitions.text: Like Antony stripped by Eros after all was lost

blocks.note: surface reading: a man undressed by the god of love
setter's reading: in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, the defeated Antony orders his servant Eros to take off his armour

explanation.surface: A romantic picture of Antony undressed by Love after losing everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Eros here is Antony's servant, not the love god: 'Unarm, Eros; the long day's task is done.'
explanation.definitionFit: Having had his armour removed, Antony was without weapons or protective gear.

clue.text: Familiarly 5 (or Old Possum's Theatre cat)

blocks.note: first meaning: a pet-name form, apparently of a name given at 5; the cross-reference is unclear in the surviving text
second meaning: the elderly stage cat in T. S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats

explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's theatre cat is called Asparagus, Gus for short. The '5' points at another entry whose short form this is, but the link does not resolve cleanly.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poem 'Gus: The Theatre Cat' names the shabby old actor cat by his nickname.

clue.text: He has a version of "The Leaping Horse"

definitions.text: He has a version of "The Leaping Horse"

blocks.clueFragment: He has a version of "The Leaping Horse"
blocks.note: surface reading: someone owns a copy of Constable's painting The Leaping Horse
setter's reading: the vaulting horse an athlete jumps over in the gym

explanation.surface: A collector owns a copy of John Constable's painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Leaping Horse' is a famous Constable landscape; the version meant is the padded vaulting apparatus.
explanation.definitionFit: This athlete performs vaults over a piece of apparatus called a horse.

clue.text: Car tiles I make of con crete

definitions.note: read as one word, concrete, an adjective

indicators.note: to make something of materials is to build it anew, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone turns car tiles into a con, or perhaps into concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is split to disguise it: 'con crete' is concrete, meaning real and tangible.
explanation.definitionFit: Concrete in the sense of solid and true to life matches a realistic, practical outlook.

clue.text: Wrong name for an Amazon

blocks.note: surface reading: a misnamed river or warrior woman
setter's reading: a girl's name that means peace, quite wrong for a warrior woman

explanation.surface: A mistaken name given to a legendary warrior woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' tempts an anagram, but there is no fodder: the name comes from Greek eirene, meaning peace.
explanation.definitionFit: The name derives from the Greek goddess of peace, ill-suited to a fierce female warrior.

clue.text: Makes no sense of

blocks.note: surface reading: fails to understand something
setter's reading: leaves without feeling, taking away the sense of touch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sense' suggests meaning, but it is bodily sensation, which cold or anaesthetic removes.
explanation.definitionFit: To numb something is to deprive it of sensation or feeling.

clue.text: Set course for the Horn?

blocks.note: first meaning: to direct a vessel or vehicle
second meaning: a young bullock, an animal with horns

explanation.surface: A sailor sets a heading for Cape Horn.
explanation.walkthrough: The Horn suggests Cape Horn, the ship's destination, but the second meaning is a horned animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Steering means guiding a course, and a steer is a castrated young male bovine bearing horns.

clue.text: Of the Vale, turn to Map 10 E

indicators.note: turning something over changes how it lies, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
the number written out as a word
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction in a guidebook to look up the valley on a map grid reference.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vale of Tempe is a famous valley in Greece, praised by poets as an ideal of beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, or by extension idyllically beautiful.

clue.text: Sprint for the papers

blocks.note: surface reading: a dash to fetch or deliver the newspapers
setter's reading: this short word placed before 'sprint' makes the paper newspapers are printed on

explanation.surface: A quick run out to collect the morning newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: NEW + SPRINT = NEWSPRINT, the cheap paper used for newspapers; the answer is what goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning fresh or recent completes the word for cheap newspaper stock.

clue.text: "The grave's a fine and private place, But none I think do there " (Marvell)

definitions.text: "The grave's a fine and private place, But none I think do there " (Marvell)

blocks.clueFragment: The grave's a fine and private place, But none I think do there
blocks.note: surface reading: lines from Andrew Marvell's poem 'To His Coy Mistress'
setter's reading: supply the missing last word of the couplet

explanation.surface: Marvell urges his reluctant lover that the tomb is no place for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the couplet from 'To His Coy Mistress' ends with this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvell's point is that in the grave nobody holds a lover close, so the rhyme word is a hug.

clue.text: Any antique does, to furnish

blocks.note: an antique has lasted, so it survives the years

explanation.surface: Any old piece of furniture will do to fit out a room.
explanation.walkthrough: The likeliest reading is ENDURE less its R; no removal signal survives in the printed text, so something may have been lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Endue is an old verb meaning to provide or endow someone with a quality or possession.

clue.text: 'Twas stormy and somewhat wet on the lake

indicators.note: a stormy sea is thrown about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
the stuff that makes things wet

explanation.surface: A wild, damp day out on the water, in the style of an old ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: Wast Water is the deepest lake in England, in the Lake District of Cumbria.
explanation.definitionFit: Wast Water is a lake in Cumbria's Wasdale, the deepest in England.
